analysis.one_liner: Sends new federal money to Medicaid home care, raises pay for care workers, and ends waiting lists for home-based help for seniors and people with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 151 cosponsors and a companion in the Senate, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on June 24-25, 2021, and never received a hearing markup or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently increased the federal government's share of Medicaid spending on home- and community-based care by 10 percentage points for states that expand access and raise care worker pay. States would have had to cut waiting lists, cover personal care for more people, support family caregivers, and pass payment increases through to home care workers' wages. It also made permanent the Money Follows the Person program that helps people move out of nursing homes, and permanent protections against 'spousal impoverishment' so a husband or wife isn't forced into poverty for a partner to get care at home.
analysis.who_benefits: Older adults and people with disabilities who need help bathing, dressing, and living at home — including hundreds of thousands on state waiting lists — would gain access to care at home instead of nursing homes. The roughly 4.6 million direct care workers, most of them women and disproportionately women of color, would benefit from required wage increases and benefits. Family caregivers would gain respite and support, and spouses would no longer face impoverishment rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, disabled people, and underpaid home care workers

how_it_helps.text: Permanently raises the federal share of Medicaid funding for home- and community-based care by 10 percentage points (up to 95%) for states that meet access and workforce benchmarks.

Requires participating states to expand financial eligibility to federal limits, cover personal care for all eligible populations, reduce waiting lists and disparities, and support family caregivers, including respite and paid family caregiving.

Requires states to raise and regularly update provider payment rates and to pass increases through to direct care worker wages, with the goal that a majority of workers earn competitive wages and benefits.

Makes the Money Follows the Person program permanent and permanently protects the spouses of home care recipients from spousal impoverishment, so families don't have to impoverish themselves to get care at home.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and to a lesser degree states, bear the cost of the permanently higher Medicaid matching rate and grant programs — financed by federal taxpayers. Institutional care providers such as nursing homes would face increased competition as care shifts to home and community settings.

drawbacks.text: The bill is expensive: it raises the federal Medicaid matching rate by 10 percentage points for home care in every participating state, appropriates $100 million for planning grants, and makes Money Follows the Person permanent at $450 million per year — a substantial, largely open-ended federal spending commitment.

Requirements fall heavily on states: to keep the extra federal money, states must maintain effort, expand eligibility to federal limits, guarantee personal care coverage, meet benchmarks for direct-care wages, and demonstrate increased service availability by their seventh year — burdens a state failing to meet could cost it the enhanced funding.

A large share of Medicaid home care is delivered through private agencies and managed care companies, and the bill routes new federal dollars through those intermediaries; it requires rate pass-throughs to workers to counter this, but relies on state enforcement to make the wage gains real.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost was money: a permanent 10-point bump in the federal matching rate for home care is a large, ongoing federal (and some state) commitment, and critics would note that federal matching dollars flow partly through provider agencies and managed care plans before reaching workers. The benefit side is concrete and large: millions of older and disabled people wait years for care, hundreds of thousands sit on waiting lists, and the direct care workforce — overwhelmingly women of color earning near-poverty wages — would see wages tied to benchmark requirements. On balance the bill's benefits to ordinary people outweighed its fiscal cost, but it was never debated, so the tradeoff was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee the day after introduction, and it never advanced to a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced H.R. 4131 on June 24, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day.
On June 25, 2021, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it sat for the remainder of the Congress with no further action listed.
151 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from one party; no Republican cosponsors are listed on the bill page.

The full action history shows only introduction, committee referral, and subcommittee referral — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote in either chamber across the entire 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home care agencies, managed care companies, and nursing homes that benefit from Medicaid home care remaining underfunded; families and disabled people on waiting lists gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing homes and home care middlemen

for.role: Original cosponsors, including the Energy and Commerce chairman

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors are listed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on June 25, 2021, and never scheduled a markup or committee vote on it during the 117th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the large new federal home care spending when it was included in the Build Back Better package, which died in the Senate without Republican support.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Announced in December 2021 that he could not support the Build Back Better Act, which contained the home care investment and effectively ended its prospects in that Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 151 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support listed; the broader home care push in the Build Back Better package also split entirely along party lines.

industries.industry: Direct care workers (home health aides, personal care attendants)
industries.note: States must show that rate increases are passed through to worker wages and that a majority of direct care workers earn competitive wages and benefits, addressing a workforce with very low pay and high turnover.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and Medicaid managed care companies
industries.note: Higher payment rates and expanded home-based services channel more public money through private agencies and managed care plans that deliver Medicaid home care; the bill requires wage pass-through and managed care rate pass-throughs but these firms remain the delivery channel.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care
industries.note: The bill rebalances Medicaid long-term care away from institutions toward home and community settings, shifting revenue toward home care and away from facilities that profit from institutional placement.
States gain a permanent 10-point boost in federal matching funds for home care, but must accept federal requirements on eligibility, rates, wage pass-through, and reporting to get it.
